QF.id: XIII Introduction to Forwards and Futures_3

question.text: What is the 'cost of carry' model for equity futures pricing?

answer.text: F = S(1 + r - q)^T (discrete) or F = S x e^((r - q) x T) (continuous), where S is spot, r is the risk-free rate, q is the dividend yield, and T is time to expiry
F = S × (1 + RINR) / (1 + RUSD) — the interest rate parity formula
F = S + Storage costs - Convenience yield

explanation.text: The Logic: For equity futures the cost-of-carry model gives F = S(1 + r - q)^T discretely, or F = S x e^((r - q) x T) under continuous compounding (with the simple approximation F = S[1 + (r - q) x T]). Carrying the stock to expiry costs the risk-free rate r and earns the dividend yield q, so dividends reduce the net carry. The Trap: The IRP form belongs to currency futures, not equity; the storage-cost form belongs to commodities; treating dividends as additive raises the futures price, which is the wrong direction. Note: Dividends enter the equity cost-of-carry model as a deduction from r, not as an addition; this is why high-yield stocks have flatter or negative futures basis.
